replies:
Good — I'll run a mock interview for a financial analyst role. I'll ask one question now; answer as you would in the room and I'll score it with one concrete improvement and then ask the next question.

First question: "Walk me through your resume — highlight the experiences that make you a strong fit for a financial analyst role."

Score: 2/10. Short summary: Structure okay but thin (1), no concrete evidence (0), low specificity (1). Top fix: add a measured result.
Rewritten answer (2–3 sentences, STAR, with placeholders you should fill): 
"At [Company], I was responsible for forecasting and financial reporting for [product/segment]. The task was to build a three-statement model to support the budgeting cycle and a potential M&A case. I gathered revenue drivers from sales and CRM, built the model in Excel using [specific functions or tools, e.g., INDEX/MATCH, SUMIFS, scenario tabs], and validated outputs by checking valuation multiples and key ratios against comps; the model shortened the budget cycle by [X weeks] and improved forecast accuracy from [A%] to [B%]."
One concrete improvement for your next answer: replace vague outcomes with one measurable result (time saved, % accuracy change, $ impact, or decision made because of your model). Now answer with that filled-in: what company/segment, what tools, and the measurable result? (one question)

Honest score: 7/10.

Why: Your filled answer shows clear structure (STAR), concrete actions (built model, gathered drivers, tools), and a measurable outcome — that meets the chief interviewer needs. It loses points where I still see vagueness: the company's name/segment, exact numbers for the measurable result, and one or two specific model details (key assumption ranges, sensitivity checks, or the exact Excel methods). Also say who used the model and what decision it changed — that pushes you from good to strong.
One-sentence tweak to push to 9/10: add the employer/segment, replace [X]/[A]/[B] with exact figures, and name one sensitivity you tested and the decision it enabled (e.g., "we ran a downside case that showed coverage dropping below 1.2x, which led management to delay the acquisition").

You’re in final rounds — good spot. I’ll prep you for technicals, behavioral stories, and questions to ask, and give a 10-minute mock you can run now. I’ll assume a direct, professional tone and that you’ll fill any [brackets] with your facts.

1) 60-second “Tell me about yourself” (speak ~55–65s)
“I’m [name], most recently [current / last title] at [company], where I focused on financial modeling, valuation and deal support for [industry or client type]. Over the past [X years/months] I built and quality-controlled 20+ three-statement and M&A models, led valuation work using DCF and precedent transactions, and supported two sell-side processes from CIM through buyer Q&A. I enjoy turning complex numbers into clear recommendations — at [last role] I streamlined our valuation template which cut model run-time and reduced post-delivery fixes. I’m focused on an execution-heavy analyst role where I can expand live-deal exposure and add to execution experience, which is why I’m excited
about Lincoln International’s mid-market M&A focus.”
Edit the bracketed facts to your specifics; keep it tight and practice to hit ~60 seconds.
2) Three behavioral stories (STAR, each with one measurable result)
- Team win — “Faster, clearer CIM valuation”
  - Situation: We had one week to finalize a CIM for a mid-market [industry] client.
  - Task: Lead the financial model, valuation and buyer list.
  - Action: Recast the model into a standardized template, ran sensitivity scenarios, coordinated research for buyer profiles, and handled late assumptions updates.
  - Result: Delivered on time; the client entered a formal bid round within two weeks / we received [X] bids / reduced model revision time by [Y hours]. (Pick the number you can cite.)
- Hard problem — “Fixing a broken model before buyer Q&A”
  - Situation: Inherited model had circularities and inconsistent assumptions ahead of Q&A.
  - Task: Restore integrity and produce reliable sensitivities.
  - Action: Isolated bad drivers, rebuilt working capital and capex schedules, added balancing checks and documentation.
  - Result: Delivered a corrected model used in Q&A; valuation gap narrowed / buyer follow-up relied on our clarifications — cite a percent or outcome.
- Failure → learning — “Missed a contract timing”
  - Situation: Early in a deal I missed a supplier renewal date that affected cash flow timing.
  - Task: Own and fix the error, and prevent recurrence.
  - Action: Notified the team, corrected projections, created a source-control checklist, instituted peer review for key assumptions.
  - Result: Avoided a material misstatement; the new checklist cut post-delivery fixes by [X%] / prevented similar issues thereafter.
3) Six short technical prompts to practice (answer aloud, 60–120s)
- Walk me through a DCF. — Project FCF, discount at WACC, compute terminal value (growth or exit multiple), sum PVs = enterprise value, adjust for cash/debt → equity value, divide by shares.
- How do you calculate WACC and what moves it? — Cost of equity via CAPM, after-tax cost of debt; weights from market cap and book debt; changes: leverage, beta, credit spread, tax rate.
- IRR vs terminal value in an LBO — IRR is annualized return driven by timing and leverage; terminal value is the exit value (multiple or perpetuity) and often dominates returns if horizon is short.
- Revenue +10% but NWC +$[X] — Higher NWC is a use of cash; initial growth can reduce FCF until working capital stabilizes.
- When to use DCF vs precedents — DCF uses company-specific cash flows; precedents show market prices — use both to triangulate and explain any gaps.
- Merger model accretion/dilution mechanics — Combine financials, adjust shares, add financing interest and synergies, compare combined EPS to acquirer EPS; drivers are purchase price, financing mix, and synergies.
4) Two sharp questions to ask interviewers
- “What does a successful analyst on this team look like in the first six months?”
- “What types of deals and industries will the team prioritize next year, and where are analysts most involved?”

5) Day-before checklist
- Confirm time, time zone, format and interviewers; ask recruiter if unknown.
- Bring or have visible model examples (screenshots or flagged sections) if asked.
- 2–3 bullet points per story with numbers accessible.
- Test video, audio, background, and phone battery; close unrelated tabs.
- Have one sentence: why Lincoln International (tie to mid-market / execution exposure).
6) 10-minute timed mock you can run now (I’ll score if you run it)
- 1 min: deliver your 60s “Tell me about yourself.”
- 2 min: answer “Walk me through a DCF.”
- 2 min: deliver the Team Win story.
- 2 min: answer “Walk me through basic accretion/dilution mechanics.”
- 3 min: ask your two questions and a close (“I’m excited about this role because [brief tie to their focus]; do you have any concerns about my fit I can address now?”)

If you run the mock here by typing your answers (paste your spoken text), I’ll score each answer for structure, evidence and specificity and give one concrete fix per answer, then the next question.
One quick next step: paste the job posting or recruiter note (if you have it) and I’ll tailor every story and the technical prompts to the posting. Is that available?

You don't have any application on file yet. The one step that starts one is: pick which posting is "the first one" — paste its link or say "search for [role] in [city]" and I'll find it and prepare the card.

Assuming I prepare the first posting you choose, here is exactly what I will put on the application card, field by field, and what I will fill vs leave for you to confirm. I assume a standard online application form; I will leave any legal or personal facts I don't already have in [brackets].

1) Employer
- What I'll put: company name exactly as on the posting.
- Source: the posting you pick.

2) Job title
- What I'll put: the posting's exact job title.
3) Location / remote flag
- What I'll put: the place or "Remote" exactly as posted.

4) Link to the application form
- What I'll put: the exact job link so the extension opens the employer's form.

5) Resume to submit
- What I'll put: the resume file you choose from your saved resumes.
- If you haven't uploaded one: the card will show an empty attachment and prompt you to paste or pick a file.
- Action for you: pick which resume to use or paste your resume now. Default if you don't answer: leave blank for you to confirm.
6) Contact name and email (top of form)
- What I'll put: the name and email exactly as you saved in your resume contact.
- If none saved: I'll leave these fields blank and mark them required for you to fill.

7) Phone number
- What I'll put: phone if you've saved it; otherwise left blank.

8) Short cover note / 120-word cover
- What I'll draft: a tailored short cover note (≤120 words) that highlights 2–3 match points from the posting and your confirmed facts.
- Brackets: any items I can't infer (notice period, salary expectation) will be left as [bracketed prompts] for you to fill.
9) Screening / eligibility questions (yes/no and short answers)
- What I'll prepare: suggested truthful answers using confirmed facts.
- Left blank/bracketed: work authorization, sponsorship needs, earliest start date, and salary expectation if not on file.

10) Attachments beyond resume
- What I'll include: any files you instruct (portfolio, transcripts). If you don't provide them, the card will list none.
- Action for you: upload any extras now or confirm none.

11) Keywords / tailoring bullets (for reviewer)
- What I'll put: 2–4 bullets showing how your resume maps to the posting (e.g., "led X project; Python, SQL; AWS").
- Purpose: helps you preview what I tailored.
12) Desired salary (if requested on form)
- What I'll put: the posting's pay if it lists one, otherwise [your desired range].
- Action for you: supply a range now or leave bracketed.

13) Work authorization / sponsorship question
- What I'll put: a drafted truthful answer from your confirmed facts; if none, left bracketed.

14) Additional employer questions (culture fit, relocation, references)
- What I'll draft: concise suggested answers; anything uncertain left bracketed.

15) Recruiter-facing private note (optional)
- What I'll draft: 1–2 short sentences highlighting the top match points to help the recruiter (visible to you on the card only).
16) Final submission checklist on the card
- What I'll show: required items left to confirm (contact email, chosen resume, bracketed answers).
- The card will show every field exactly as it will be submitted and every attachment.

17) Post-submission tracking fields (placeholders)
- What I'll prepare: fields to record submitted date, application ID, and a follow-up reminder; these remain blank until you actually send and the employer returns any IDs.
What I will not do without your explicit approval
- I will not submit the form for you. I will not send emails or connect your mailbox until you connect it and approve on the card. I will not invent dates, authorization, salary or start dates — anything missing will be bracketed for you.

Next step: paste the job link you mean by "the first one" (or say "search for [role] in [city]") and paste or point to the resume you want attached. Saved nothing yet. Is that the right plan?
